edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's wallet was stolen and a collection account for a credit card she never opened appears on her report. She files an FTC identity-theft report and disputes through Experian; the collector's ACDV 'verifies' the account because the name and SSN in its file match hers. She asks what her rights are against the furnisher.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats the CRA-forwarded dispute under § 1681s-2(b) as the only route for a 'not my account' claim and says nothing about the FCRA identity-theft track: § 1681c-2 requires a CRA to block information identified by the consumer as resulting from identity theft within 4 business days of receiving an identity-theft report, and § 1681s-2(a)(6)(B) bars a furnisher from re-reporting blocked information after it receives the block notice. Applied as encoded, the node routes an identity-theft victim into a slower, litigation-dependent, damages-limited (b) analysis with unsettled reasonable-investigation and legal/factual hurdles, and never surfaces the mandatory-block remedy that is the primary and far faster relief for this very common fact pattern. That is materially misleading advice, not merely incomplete.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer disputed a charge-off balance through TransUnion, the furnisher verified it, and she then disputed a second time attaching her bank statements and a paid-in-full settlement letter she had not previously submitted. The CRA marked the second dispute 'previously investigated / no new information' and the furnisher did nothing.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's cra_forwarding_trigger_note affirmatively states that CRAs commonly terminate 'template or duplicate disputes' as frivolous under § 1681i(a)(3), and the dispositive checklist item 1 asks only whether the CRA forwarded. Applied as encoded, a repeat dispute is likely to be closed as 'no furnisher duty ever arose.' But § 1681i(a)(3) permits a frivolousness finding based on the consumer's failure to provide sufficient information, and a re-dispute accompanied by genuinely new documentation is generally not frivolous; a CRA's mislabeling of it does not immunize either party, and the consumer may have a claim against the CRA under § 1681i for wrongly terminating. The node's own text thus points toward the wrong conclusion for the common 'I disputed again with proof' scenario.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer received a Chapter 7 discharge two years ago, but a debt buyer still reports the pre-petition credit card account with a balance owed and a 'charge-off' status. He disputes through Equifax; the furnisher verifies the balance as accurate against its own records.
edge_cases.gap_description: Post-discharge reporting of a pre-petition debt as still owing is among the most common furnisher-dispute fact patterns, and the node's legal_vs_factual_dispute_note could push this into the 'purely legal dispute / no furnisher duty' bucket, while the accuracy_element_note could push it into 'accurate reporting the consumer objects to for equitable reasons.' In fact discharge status is objectively and readily verifiable from PACER and reporting a discharged debt as an outstanding balance is a paradigm materially misleading inaccuracy (and may also implicate 11 U.S.C. § 524(a)(2)). The node is silent on this overlay.

The limits are applied per 'particular debt' — each debt in collection counts separately (except student loans serviced under one account number, which count as one debt) — and calls do not count toward the limits if they are placed with the person's prior consent given directly to the collector within the following seven days, are not connected to the dialed number, or are placed to persons described in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii)–(vi). edge_cases.scenario: A consumer brings in a phone log showing 14 calls in one week from a collection agency about a credit-card debt, but the calls occurred 16 months ago (or in 2020, before Reg F's Nov. 30, 2021 effective date); she stopped hearing from the agency after that and is only now asking whether she has a claim.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no temporal screen. It applies bankruptcy, validation-dispute, coverage, and state-law thresholds but never asks WHEN the calls occurred relative to today. results.derivation_summary: Section 1692e broadly bars a debt collector from using any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with collecting a debt, and then lists sixteen non-exhaustive examples of violations: (1) falsely implying government affiliation or bonding; (2) misrepresenting the character, amount, or legal status of a debt, or the services/compensation lawfully collectible; (3) falsely implying attorney status or attorney-sourced communications; (4) threatening arrest, imprisonment, seizure, garnishment, attachment, or sale unless lawful and actually intended; (5) threatening any action that cannot legally be taken or is not intended; (6) falsely implying a transfer of the debt strips the consumer of claims/defenses; (7) falsely implying the consumer committed a crime or disgraceful conduct; (8) communicating credit information known to be false, including failing to note a debt is disputed; (9) using written communications simulating court or government documents; (10) using any false representation or deceptive means to collect a debt or obtain consumer information; (11) failing to give the 'mini-Miranda' disclosures (with a formal-pleading exception, now implemented by 12 C.F.R. § 1006.18(e)); (12) falsely implying accounts went to innocent purchasers for value; (13) falsely implying documents are legal process; (14) using a business name other than the collector's true name; (15) falsely implying documents are not legal process or require no consumer action; and (16) falsely implying the collector is or works for a consumer reporting agency. Courts have added a judicial gloss requiring the false statement to be material — capable of influencing the consumer's decision or action regarding the debt — judged under either a 'least sophisticated consumer' or 'reasonable consumer' standard, and have applied §§ 1692e(2)(A), (5), and (10) to suits, threats, and even dunning letters on time-barred debts. Claims must be brought within one year of the violation under § 1692k(d), and a federal plaintiff must also show concrete harm under TransUnion v. Ramirez; California's Rosenthal Act (Civ. Code § 1788.17) incorporates §§ 1692b–1692j, though § 1692e(11) does not apply to persons described in § 1692a(6)(A)–(B) or their principals.

Please call us back at 555-0199 between 8am and 5pm.' No mention that the caller is a debt collector. edge_cases.gap_description: The node imports Reg F § 1006.18(e) for the mini-Miranda but never mentions Reg F § 1006.2(j)'s 'limited-content message,' which is expressly NOT a 'communication' and therefore does not trigger the § 1692e(11) initial/subsequent disclosure duty. The dispositive checklist item ('Whether the collector disclosed in EACH subsequent communication that it was a debt collector') would flag a violation on a compliant limited-content voicemail — a false positive on one of the highest-volume fact patterns in modern collection practice. Conversely, a voicemail that exceeds the limited-content safe harbor (e.g., mentions the account or the creditor) IS a communication and does require the disclosure; the node gives no way to tell the two apart.

edge_cases.scenario: A collector's letter states 'Balance due: $4,312.18' with no indication that interest and fees continue to accrue. The figure was accurate on the date of the letter; the consumer pays $4,312.18 and is then told she still owes $187 in interest that accrued after the letter. She asks whether the letter was false or deceptive.
edge_cases.gap_description: The catalog's item (2)(A) is framed as 'falsely representing the ... amount,' and the materiality note reinforces a literal-accuracy frame. It captures no 'accurate-but-misleading static balance' theory — the Avila v. Riexinger line (2d Cir.) and its progeny hold that stating a current balance without disclosing that it accrues interest/fees violates § 1692e(10), with a recognized safe-harbor disclosure. Applied as encoded, the node would tell a consumer with a very common accruing-balance dunning letter that there is no violation because the number was correct when written. The node also never states the governing objective standard (least-sophisticated/unsophisticated consumer), which is what makes literally-true-but-misleading statements actionable.

edge_cases.scenario: A third-party collector's first letter overstates the balance by $900 because the original creditor's data file mis-mapped a payment; the collector has written intake and data-verification procedures, and corrected the balance within days of the consumer's call. The consumer asks whether she has a viable § 1692e(2)(A) claim.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's determination ('any single catalog item, if the facts match, is an independent § 1692e violation') and its checklist never reference the § 1692k(c) bona fide error defense — a complete defense to liability where the error was unintentional and the collector maintained reasonably adapted procedures (limited by Jerman v. Carlisle to non-legal errors). Misstated balances traceable to creditor-supplied data are among the most common § 1692e fact patterns, and the node already extends past pure conduct into claim viability (adding SOL and standing notes), so omitting the only statutory defense that can defeat the claim outright materially overstates the consumer's position. No checklist item asks about the origin of the error or the collector's procedures.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer receives dunning letters from a debt buyer on a 9-year-old credit card debt, well past the state statute of limitations. The letters offer a settlement, disclose nothing false, and never threaten suit; separately, the same buyer filed a proof of claim on the stale debt in the consumer's Chapter 13 case. The consumer asks whether this is an 'unfair practice.'
edge_cases.gap_description: The general_clause_note affirmatively lists 'continuing to collect a debt known to be time-barred' as a § 1692f general-clause violation. That is stated too categorically: Midland Funding v. Johnson (2017) held that filing a proof of claim on a time-barred debt is neither 'unfair' nor 'unconscionable' under the FDCPA, and most circuits hold that merely dunning (without suing or threatening suit, and without misrepresenting enforceability) a time-barred debt is not a § 1692f violation — the viable theory is usually § 1692e deception about enforceability or revival risk. As encoded, the node tells a very common 'zombie debt' consumer they have a § 1692f claim that courts would reject.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer whose Chapter 7 debts were discharged two years ago keeps getting collection calls and letters from a third-party collector on a discharged medical bill. She wants to know whether she can sue under the FDCPA in federal court in California.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's general_clause_note states categorically that 'continuing to collect a debt known to be discharged in bankruptcy' violates § 1692f. This is the node's own affirmative (not silent) statement and it is wrong in a large part of the country: the Ninth Circuit (Walls v. Wells Fargo) and several other courts hold that an FDCPA claim premised on a discharge violation is precluded by 11 U.S.C. § 524's exclusive contempt remedy, while the Second Circuit (Garfield v. Ocwen) allows it. A consumer in a preclusion circuit would be told to file an FDCPA suit that will be dismissed, when the correct route is a motion to reopen and a contempt motion under § 524/Taggart.

edge_cases.scenario: A collection agency's repo agent, holding a valid auto security agreement with the borrower in default, cuts the padlock on the consumer's fenced yard and tows the car while the consumer stands in the driveway shouting objections. The consumer asks whether the repossession was lawful under the FDCPA.
edge_cases.gap_description: Catalog item (6) and its checklist question ask only whether the collector had a 'present legal right,' present intent, and whether the property is exempt. It omits the breach-of-the-peace condition: under UCC § 9-609 self-help repossession is privileged only if done without breach of the peace, and courts routinely hold that a repo conducted over the debtor's contemporaneous objection or by breaking a barrier destroys the 'present right to possession' and violates § 1692f(6). Applied as encoded, the node answers 'no item (6) violation — the collector had a present enforceable right,' which is the wrong answer in one of the most common repossession fact patterns.

results.derivation_summary: Under §1692a(6), a "debt collector" is a person whose business's principal purpose is collecting debts, or who regularly collects debts "owed or due another" — so under Henson, an entity collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not covered by that second prong, while §1692a(4) excludes from "creditor" anyone taking assignment of a debt already in default solely to collect for another. Coverage also requires a "debt" under §1692a(5): a consumer's obligation to pay money arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes (so business/commercial obligations fall outside), owed by a "consumer" natural person under §1692a(3). The definition contains exclusions (A)–(F), including creditor employees collecting in the creditor's name, affiliated collectors, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, and persons collecting debts they originated or that were not in default when obtained; but a creditor using a false third-party name is pulled back in. Finally, per the third sentence of §1692a(6) and Obduskey, one engaged in no more than security-interest enforcement (e.g., nonjudicial foreclosure) is a debt collector only for purposes of §1692f(6).

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer verbally lent (or borrowed) $6,000 from a friend with no repayment date agreed -- 'pay me back when you can.' Three years later the lender demanded repayment, was refused, and sued 18 months after that refusal. The consumer asks whether the suit is time-barred.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's accrual definition ('date of default/breach or last payment') gives no rule for the paradigm case it says it exists to cover: an unwritten loan with no stated due date. California treats a loan with no fixed repayment date as payable on demand or within a reasonable time, and courts frequently fix accrual at or shortly after the making of the loan rather than at the date the lender finally demanded repayment. Applied as encoded, the node would take the refusal date as the breach and report a suit filed 18 months later as timely, when the claim may well have accrued years earlier and be barred -- the dangerous direction (consumer abandons a good defense). Neither the logic nor the checklist asks whether a repayment date was ever set or when demand was made.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a purely verbal $4,000 personal loan in March 2021, then made a single unsolicited $200 payment in January 2023 (within the 2-year period) with no signed writing of any kind. The lender sued in June 2024. The consumer asks if the suit is time-barred.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's accrual rule expressly uses 'the date of default/breach or LAST PAYMENT,' which would run the 2-year clock from January 2023 and report the June 2024 suit as timely. But CCP § 360 requires a signed writing for any acknowledgment or new promise, and its payment proviso is limited to promissory notes -- an unwritten obligation is not one. The node itself acknowledges this for POST-expiration payments (the § 360 revival note and checklist item 6) but leaves the affirmative 'last payment restarts the clock' rule in place for PRE-expiration payments, where the same writing requirement applies. This is the node's own text stating something wrong, and it errs in the dangerous direction: telling a consumer with a likely-complete SOL defense that the suit is timely.

edge_cases.scenario: A patient/homeowner had a purely verbal arrangement with a dentist (or a contractor/small supplier) who provided services over many months and kept a running ledger of charges, credits, and partial payments. The provider sued 3 years after the last charge; the consumer, told the agreement was never in writing, asks whether the 2-year oral period bars the suit.
edge_cases.gap_description: An 'open book account' under CCP § 337(a)(2) carries a 4-year period regardless of whether the underlying agreement was written or oral -- a running account of debits and credits on an oral services arrangement is the classic book account. The node's classification_note and checklist item 3 frame the book-account/account-stated escape hatch exclusively as a credit-card/revolving-account issue ('cardmember agreement, account terms'), so a user with an oral services debt is routed into the 2-year period and told 'expired' when a 4-year period likely applies. That is the dangerous direction: false confidence in a defense that will fail, and no prompt to check whether the creditor kept a running account.

edge_cases.scenario: A minimum-wage-plus retail worker in Los Angeles asks how much her creditor can take. Her paystub shows $780 gross, and $612 net after federal/state tax, SDI, her employer health-plan premium, a 401(k) contribution, and union dues. She (and the node's checklist, which just asks for 'weekly disposable earnings') plugs in $612 as her disposable earnings.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node never defines 'disposable earnings.' Under CCP § 706.011(a)/706.025 it is gross earnings minus amounts REQUIRED by law to be withheld (taxes, SDI, mandatory retirement) — voluntary deductions such as health premiums, 401(k) elective deferrals, union dues and wage assignments are NOT subtracted. A user supplying net take-home pay gets a materially wrong dollar figure in both prongs of the formula, and would wrongly conclude a lawful withholding was excessive (or that a partly excessive one was lawful). Because the checklist marks this input dispositive but supplies no definition, the error is systematic, not incidental.

edge_cases.gap_description: The node's determination ('anything withheld beyond that is unlawful') and its only priority carve-out (support orders) omit federal administrative garnishments and IRS/FTB levies, which are not subject to CCP § 706.050 and take priority over a consumer EWO (see CCP § 706.023(b), §§ 706.072-706.080; 20 U.S.C. § 1095a; 26 U.S.C. § 6331/6334(d)). This is a distinct priority stream from the support-order note already added, and defaulted federal student loans plus a card judgment is a very common pairing.

edge_cases.scenario: A homeowner with $250,000 of equity (well under the exemption) has an abstract of judgment recorded against her by a credit-card creditor. She is not being levied on; she wants to refinance or sell voluntarily, and escrow/title tells her the judgment lien must be paid off before the deal can close.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats the exemption as a blanket 'your equity is protected,' but the homestead exemption only defeats a FORCED SALE; a recorded abstract of judgment still attaches to and encumbers the homestead under CCP 697.310 and must be dealt with on a voluntary sale or refinance. The only partial relief -- CCP 704.950, under which a judgment lien attaches to a DECLARED homestead only to the extent of surplus over liens plus the exemption -- and the CCP 704.960/704.980 mechanism are not encoded. A debtor told her equity is 'protected' will be blindsided at escrow, and will not learn that recording a homestead declaration beforehand is what limits the lien. Neither the forced-sale-mechanics note (704.800) nor the sale-proceeds note addresses lien attachment to title.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor moved out of the house 14 months ago (job relocation / moved in with an adult child / entered assisted living) and now rents it out, but still calls it 'my home' and has never bought another residence. A judgment creditor applies for an order of sale. Alternatively, the debtor moved into the house only after the creditor's judgment lien attached to it.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist reduces the threshold question to 'occupied dwelling' and expressly punts ('not itself encoded in this node'). CCP 704.710(c) requires that the debtor or the debtor's spouse resided in the dwelling when the judgment creditor's lien attached AND resided there continuously thereafter until the court determines the dwelling is a homestead. A former resident who is now a landlord has no automatic homestead exemption at all, yet the encoded rule -- keyed to a lay 'is it your home' question -- will tell that person a $300k-$600k+ exemption protects them. The temporal/continuous-residence element, and the fact that a spouse's residence suffices while a non-spouse relative's does not, are entirely missing.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor is served with a judgment creditor's application for an order of sale of the dwelling and an order to show cause. Believing the homestead exemption is automatic and self-executing, she does not appear; the creditor's appraisal values the home $150,000 above what she believes it is worth, and the court sets a minimum bid on that basis and orders the sale.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node and checklist encode only the substantive amount and the 704.800 minimum-bid arithmetic, with no procedure: the CCP 704.740-704.780 application/OSC process, the debtor's obligation to file a timely notice of opposition and claim of exemption, the court-appointed appraisal and the debtor's right to contest valuation, and the consequences of default. Because the encoded output is 'equity up to the exemption is protected,' a debtor is affirmatively encouraged to be passive at exactly the moment when appearance and a competing appraisal are what determine whether the sale happens and how much she keeps.

gaps_found.scenario: A homeowner with $250,000 of equity (well under the exemption) has an abstract of judgment recorded against her by a credit-card creditor. She is not being levied on; she wants to refinance or sell voluntarily, and escrow/title tells her the judgment lien must be paid off before the deal can close.
gaps_found.gap_description: The node treats the exemption as a blanket 'your equity is protected,' but the homestead exemption only defeats a FORCED SALE; a recorded abstract of judgment still attaches to and encumbers the homestead under CCP 697.310 and must be dealt with on a voluntary sale or refinance. The only partial relief -- CCP 704.950, under which a judgment lien attaches to a DECLARED homestead only to the extent of surplus over liens plus the exemption -- and the CCP 704.960/704.980 mechanism are not encoded. A debtor told her equity is 'protected' will be blindsided at escrow, and will not learn that recording a homestead declaration beforehand is what limits the lien. Neither the forced-sale-mechanics note (704.800) nor the sale-proceeds note addresses lien attachment to title.

gaps_found.gap_description: The checklist reduces the threshold question to 'occupied dwelling' and expressly punts ('not itself encoded in this node'). CCP 704.710(c) requires that the debtor or the debtor's spouse resided in the dwelling when the judgment creditor's lien attached AND resided there continuously thereafter until the court determines the dwelling is a homestead. edge_cases.scenario: A debtor with one paid-off car worth $12,000 is served with a notice of levy. He reads that with only one vehicle the $7,500 exemption 'applies automatically without filing a claim,' so he files nothing; the sheriff sells the car and mails him $7,500. He wanted to keep the car (and could have raised tools-of-trade or negotiated to pay the excess), and the automatic rule of § 704.010(d) protected only the sale proceeds, never the vehicle itself.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's 'automatic_single_vehicle_case' field, and the deadline note's express carve-out ('except in the single-vehicle automatic-proceeds case'), tell the modal single-car debtor that no claim of exemption is needed. In fact § 704.010(d) only makes the exemption attach to the proceeds of the execution sale; it does not prevent seizure or sale, and a debtor whose equity exceeds $7,500 who does nothing loses the vehicle. The node should require a claim of exemption (and § 704.800 / excess-payment options) even in the one-vehicle case, treating (d) purely as a proceeds backstop.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment creditor levies on a car parked at the debtor's home that is titled jointly to the debtor and his mother (who co-signed and made the down payment), or titled solely to his adult son. The debtor is told $7,500 of the car's equity is protected and the rest is reachable.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no ownership/title variable: its checklist collects only FMV and amounts owed, and its community-property note addresses spouses only (CCP 703.110). For a non-spouse co-owner, only the debtor's fractional interest is leviable, and where the true owner is a third party the correct remedy is a third-party claim under CCP §§ 720.110 et seq. (which can defeat the levy entirely), not a $7,500 exemption claim. Applying the node as encoded materially understates protection and points the debtor to the wrong procedure and the wrong deadline.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment is entered against a small contractor's LLC (or against a sole proprietor's incorporated business) and the sheriff levies on a work truck titled to the entity. The owner asks whether the $7,500 vehicle exemption protects it.
edge_cases.gap_description: CCP § 703.020 limits the § 704 exemptions to property of a natural person; an entity judgment debtor gets no vehicle exemption at all. The node contains no natural-person / entity-debtor screen, so it would tell an LLC or corporate debtor that $7,500 of truck equity is protected when the correct answer is zero — a flatly wrong result that could cause the debtor to forgo the real options (bond/undertaking, negotiated release, or the owner's separate personally-titled vehicle).

edge_cases.scenario: A defendant who says the papers were left at her mother's old address follows the node's advice and files a CCP § 418.10 motion to quash on day 25. She then asks whether she also has to file an answer by day 30 to avoid default, and what happens to her deadline if the motion is denied.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node affirmatively directs disputing defendants to the § 418.10 motion-to-quash route but encodes only one deadline formula (service + 30 days) and one consequence (default). It never states that a timely motion to quash filed on or before the last day to plead SUSPENDS the obligation to answer, and that under § 418.10(b) the defendant gets 15 days after service of notice of denial (plus tolling during any writ petition) to plead. Applied as encoded, the rule tells this defendant her answer is still due on day 30 -- pushing her to file the very general appearance the node elsewhere warns waives her jurisdictional objection, or to believe she is in default when she is not.

edge_cases.scenario: A defendant sued by a debt buyer on a charged-off credit card whose last payment was seven years ago files a timely general-denial answer (PLD-050) on day 28 without listing any affirmative defenses, then tries to raise the four-year statute of limitations at trial.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats 'file an answer by day 30' as the complete safe response, but says nothing about the answer's required CONTENT. Under CCP § 431.30(b)(2) affirmative defenses -- most importantly the statute of limitations, the single most common winning defense in stale-debt suits and the subject of a companion node -- are waived if not pled in the answer (subject only to discretionary leave to amend). A defendant who follows the node's guidance exactly can timely answer and still forfeit the defense that would have ended the case, which is a materially misleading result for this node's core audience.

edge_cases.scenario: A legal-aid-assisted defendant files a demurrer (or motion to strike) on day 27 attacking a debt-buyer complaint that pleads a common count with no account documents. The demurrer is overruled two months later, and the defendant asks whether default can be taken because day 30 came and went.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's universe of responses is 'answer' or 'motion to quash.' It omits that a demurrer or motion to strike is itself a timely responsive pleading that stops the default clock, and that under CCP § 472a(b) the time to answer runs 10 days from notice of the ruling (or the period the court sets), not from the original service date. As encoded, the rule tells a defendant who properly demurred that she blew her deadline and is exposed to default -- a wrong answer that could cause her to abandon a meritorious pleading challenge or file a redundant answer.

results.derivation_summary: Under the Texas Constitution, article XVI, section 28, current wages for personal service can never be garnished, with only two exceptions: court-ordered child support and court-ordered spousal maintenance. Ordinary consumer debts are not among those exceptions, so a consumer creditor cannot garnish wages. This is reinforced by Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 63.004, which exempts current wages from garnishment and requires the garnishee (employer) to be discharged as to any current-wage debt, and by § 31.0025(a), which bars a court from ordering turnover of wages before they are paid. Employers likewise may only withhold wages under a court order, other legal authorization, or the employee's written authorization (Tex. Lab. Code § 61.018).

edge_cases.scenario: A Texas debtor with a default judgment from a credit card issuer has her bank account frozen by writ of garnishment. The account holds her Texas unemployment benefits (Tex. Lab. Code § 207.075) and, at another bank, an IRA/401(k) rollover held in a bank-custodied account (Tex. Prop. Code § 42.0021). She asks whether the freeze is proper.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node states bank funds 'CAN generally be frozen/seized' and qualifies that statement only for directly-deposited federal benefits (SSA/SSDI/VA under 42 U.S.C. 407 and 31 C.F.R. Part 212). It is silent on the substantial body of TEXAS statutory exemptions that also protect deposited funds -- unemployment compensation (Lab. Code § 207.075), workers' compensation benefits (Lab. Code § 408.201), and retirement/IRA funds (Prop. Code § 42.0021), plus proceeds of exempt property. A debtor whose frozen account holds these would be told the seizure is 'fair game' and would fail to file the timely claim of exemption / motion to dissolve (TRCP 664a) that is her actual remedy. This is a different exemption source than the federal-benefit carve-out already fixed in D-01.

edge_cases.scenario: A Texas father's employer receives an income withholding order for child support arrears and begins withholding roughly 70% of his disposable earnings, leaving him unable to pay rent. He asks whether anything can be done, since he has heard Texas bans wage garnishment.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats 'court-ordered child support' and 'spousal maintenance' as flat, unqualified exceptions, so as encoded it returns 'garnishable -- no protection.' That is materially misleading: Tex. Fam. Code § 158.009 caps withholding at 50% of disposable earnings (and Tex. Fam. Code § 8.106 caps maintenance withholding at 20% of average monthly gross income; the federal CCPA, 15 U.S.C. § 1673(b), also caps support garnishment at 50-65%). Over-withholding is a very common real dispute, and the debtor's remedy is a motion to modify/correct the withholding order -- not acquiescence. Neither the logic nor the checklist contains any amount-limit fact.

edge_cases.scenario: A Texas debtor's paycheck is direct-deposited on Friday; the judgment creditor serves a bank garnishment the following Monday and the entire deposited paycheck is frozen. He argues the money is still 'current wages for personal service' and therefore constitutionally exempt.

results.derivation_summary: Under Tex. Prop. Code § 41.001(a), a Texas homestead (and burial lots) is exempt from seizure for creditors' claims, except for encumbrances properly fixed on the homestead; § 41.002 caps the exemption at 10 acres for an urban home, and for a rural home 200 acres for a family or 100 acres for a single adult. The character of the homestead is preserved despite temporary renting if no other homestead is acquired (§ 41.003), can be held through a 'qualifying trust' (§ 41.0021), and a judgment debtor may file an affidavit in the county real property records that operates as a release of a judgment lien against the homestead (§ 52.0012(b)-(c)). The exemption is not absolute: in bankruptcy the state exemption applies only if the debtor's domicile was in Texas for the 730 days before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)), and it is limited by § 522(p)'s cap on homestead interest acquired within 1,215 days before filing ($250,000 statutory base, currently adjusted to $214,000 for cases filed April 1, 2025 through March 31, 2028) and § 522(o)'s reduction for value traceable to property disposed of within 10 years with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud creditors. Separately, a federal tax lien under 26 U.S.C. § 6321 attaches to all property of the taxpayer, and United States v. Rodgers, 461 U.S. 677 (1983), held that such a lien reaches homestead property despite the state exemption under the Supremacy Clause, permitting a federal court to order a judicial sale.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment creditor obtains a writ of execution and a constable levies on the debtor's pickup truck and household furniture, and separately the debtor's bank is served with a writ of garnishment freezing the account. The debtor, told by the rule that these items are exempt, does nothing and does not file a claim of exemption, motion to dissolve, or answer in the garnishment proceeding before the deadline.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node encodes only the substantive exemption and is silent that Texas exemptions are not self-executing in post-judgment enforcement: the debtor must timely assert the exemption (claim of exemption/motion to dissolve or vacate the writ, answer in garnishment under TRCP 664a/658-679) or the exempt property can be sold or the frozen funds turned over. For the modal user -- a person whose car or account has just been levied on -- 'your property is exempt' without 'and you must affirmatively claim it, on a deadline' is materially misleading and can produce actual loss of property the statute protects. Neither the logic nor any of the 14 checklist items mentions procedure, deadlines, or who bears the burden of claiming the exemption.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor with a default judgment against her is receiving Texas workers' compensation income benefits (or state unemployment benefits) by direct deposit; the creditor garnishes the bank account, and the creditor also serves the workers' comp carrier. Applying the node, she is told these are not on the § 42.002(a) list and the deposited funds are not federal benefits, so they are reachable.
edge_cases.gap_description: The enumerated-list gate note and checklist item 2 tell the user that anything not on the § 42.002(a) list -- including bank deposits -- is '100% reachable,' subject only to the node's own enumerated 'other specific exemptions,' and checklist item 12 asks only about federal benefits (Social Security/VA). Texas workers' compensation benefits (Tex. Lab. Code § 408.201) and unemployment compensation benefits (Tex. Lab. Code § 207.075) are exempt from garnishment/attachment under state law and generally retain protection when identifiable, as are certain public retirement/annuity payments (e.g., Gov't Code ch. 811/831 teacher and state employee benefits). The node's affirmative 'not exempt' framing for non-listed assets makes this a wrong answer, not merely a silent one, for a large and sympathetic slice of Texas judgment debtors.

edge_cases.scenario: A married Texas debtor is sued alone on a credit card she opened before the marriage; the creditor gets a judgment and garnishes a joint bank account and seeks to seize a second vehicle and furniture that her husband owns as separate property or that he alone manages. She asks whether anything beyond the $100,000 family cap can be taken.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's analysis is purely 'is the item listed and is aggregate value under the cap,' with no marital-property liability screen. In a community-property state, which property is even subject to the judgment is often the dispositive question: under Tex. Fam. Code §§ 3.202 and 3.203, a non-debtor spouse's separate property and (for a premarital or non-necessaries tort debt) the non-debtor spouse's sole-management community property are not liable at all, and creditors must observe the order-of-resort rules. Telling a married debtor that all listed property above the cap and all bank funds are seizable overstates exposure in one common direction and understates it in another (community property of the debtor spouse being reachable even if titled to the other spouse). No checklist item asks about marital status for liability purposes -- item 1 asks about 'family' status only to set the dollar cap.

edge_cases.scenario: A caller was served with a JP-court debt-claim citation, did nothing, and a default judgment was signed three weeks ago; she found out when her bank account was frozen. She asks what her deadline is now.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's only post-deadline branch is 'has a default been signed? if not, answer now.' It is silent on the far more common 'yes, it was signed' branch, where distinct and short deadlines control: motion for new trial within 14 days of judgment (TRCP 505.3), appeal de novo to county court within 21 days (TRCP 506.1), plus restricted appeal/bill of review for defective service. Applied as encoded, the node dead-ends a defendant who still has a live, time-sensitive remedy, and the 14/21-day clocks can run out while she believes nothing can be done.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sued a Houston-area consumer in a JP precinct on the other side of the county (or a neighboring county) where he has never lived and never signed anything. Following the node, he files a general written answer on day 12 to avoid default.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node treats 'file an answer' as the only step tied to the 14-day deadline. Under TRCP 502.4(d) a justice-court motion to transfer venue must be filed before or concurrently with any other plea or pleading (other than a special appearance); filing a bare general answer first waives the improper-venue objection. Wrong-precinct filing by debt buyers is a well-documented pattern (and a 15 U.S.C. 1692i issue), so the node's advice can cause a defendant to forfeit a real, commonly available defense at the very moment it instructs him to act.

edge_cases.scenario: A tenant is handed a JP-court citation from her landlord over $3,400 in unpaid rent; the papers are an eviction (forcible detainer) petition seeking possession plus back rent, with a trial setting stamped on the citation. She asks how long she has to answer the 'debt lawsuit.'
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist's only court question is JP vs. county/district; it never asks the CASE TYPE. Eviction suits are filed in the same JP courts but are governed by TRCP 510, under which trial is set roughly 10-21 days out, no written answer is required, and the dispositive obligation is to APPEAR at the trial setting -- non-appearance yields immediate default judgment for possession. Telling such a defendant she has '14 days to file an answer' can cause her to miss the trial date and lose possession.
